_comment: Pearson Edexcel GCSE (9-1) English Language 1EN0. SOURCE OF FACTS: component titles, paper codes, durations, mark totals, weightings, text centuries, word counts and the AO weightings were read from the official Pearson specification (Issue 6, August 2024). The per-question marks and the section timings were read from real Edexcel question papers: 1EN0/01 November 2017 and 1EN0/02 November 2021. Paper 1 Section A is 1+2+6+15=24 and Section B is 40, giving 64. Paper 2 Section A is 2+2+15+1+1+6+14=56 and Section B is 40, giving 96. Both totals match the figures printed on the papers. No Edexcel question, source text or mark scheme wording is reproduced; all examples and practice are original RCF English work.

hero.text: Two papers of very different length and weight. Paper 2 is worth 60% of the qualification and runs for two hours and five minutes, which surprises students who have been revising both papers equally.

blocks.text: **Pearson Edexcel GCSE (9-1) English Language, specification 1EN0, is assessed by two written papers.** Paper 1 lasts 1 hour 45 minutes, carries 64 marks and is worth 40%. Paper 2 lasts 2 hours 5 minutes, carries 96 marks and is worth 60%. Spoken Language is assessed separately and does not count towards the 9-1 grade.

blocks.title: Where these figures come from
text: The component titles, paper codes, durations, mark totals, weightings and text centuries were read from Pearson's own [1EN0 specification](https://qualifications.pearson.com/en/qualifications/edexcel-gcses/english-language-2015.html), Issue 6, August 2024.
The marks for each individual question and the section timings were read from real Edexcel question papers. They add up to the totals printed on those papers, which is the check that matters.
**RCF English is not affiliated with, endorsed by or approved by Pearson Edexcel.** No Edexcel question, source text or mark scheme wording is reproduced anywhere on this site.

blocks.title: A note on the code 1EN0
text: **1EN0 is the GCSE English Language taken in schools in England.** It is sometimes confused with *English Language A*, which is a different qualification: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE English Language A, code **4EA1**, taken in international schools.
If your statement of entry says 1EN0 you are in the right place. If it says 4EA1, see the [International GCSE page](global-english/igcse/) instead.

blocks.title: The single most important difference from AQA
text: On AQA the two papers are worth 50% each. **On Edexcel they are not.** Paper 2 carries 96 of the 160 marks - 60% of the qualification - and runs twenty minutes longer.

If you are revising Edexcel and dividing your time equally between the papers, you are giving Paper 1 half your effort for 40% of the marks. See [how AQA and Edexcel differ](global-english/gcse/) for the other contrasts.

blocks.heading: The assessment objectives and their weightings
text: Pearson publishes the percentage each objective carries across the whole qualification. Two things stand out: writing is 50% of the marks between AO5 and AO6, and AO4 - evaluation - is the largest single reading objective.
bullets: **AO1** - identify and interpret information and ideas, and synthesise evidence from different texts. **9.4%**
**AO2** - explain, comment on and analyse how writers use language and structure. **13.1%**
**AO3** - compare writers' ideas and perspectives across two or more texts. **8.8%**
**AO4** - evaluate texts critically, supported by references. **18.8%**
**AO5** - communicate clearly and imaginatively; organise ideas. **30%**
**AO6** - range of vocabulary and sentence structures, with accurate spelling and punctuation. **20%**
**AO7 to AO9** cover the Spoken Language endorsement and carry no weighting towards the grade.

blocks.title: Questions marked with an asterisk
text: Edexcel papers mark some questions with an asterisk. On those questions the quality of your written communication is assessed as well as the content, so spelling, punctuation, grammar and clarity carry weight. The paper tells you which questions these are - check before you write.

blocks.heading: Spoken Language endorsement
text: Paper code 1EN0/03. One prepared presentation of up to ten minutes, in a formal setting, followed by questions and feedback. There are no marks: students are awarded Pass, Merit or Distinction, reported separately on the certificate. It is 0% of the GCSE grade.

blocks.heading: Questions about Edexcel GCSE English Language

items.q: How long is Edexcel English Language Paper 2?
a: 2 hours 5 minutes, for 96 marks. The paper advises spending about 1 hour 20 minutes on Section A and about 45 minutes on Section B. Paper 1 is shorter at 1 hour 45 minutes for 64 marks.

items.q: Which Edexcel English Language paper is worth more?
a: Paper 2, by a considerable margin. It carries 96 of the 160 marks - 60% of the GCSE - while Paper 1 carries 64 marks and 40%. Paper 2 also has more questions and runs twenty minutes longer.

items.q: What is Question 7 on Edexcel Paper 2?
a: It is the only question that uses both texts, and it comes in two parts worth 20 marks together. Question 7(a) is worth 6 marks and asks what similarities the two texts share, using evidence from both. Question 7(b) is worth 14 marks and asks you to compare how the writers present their ideas and perspectives.

items.q: Is there a 19th-century text on Edexcel Paper 2?
a: No. Edexcel puts its 19th-century text on Paper 1, where the reading extract is 19th-century fiction of about 650 words. Paper 2 uses two unseen non-fiction extracts from the 20th and 21st centuries, one of which is literary non-fiction. This is a real difference from AQA, whose Paper 2 pairs a 19th-century source with a modern one.

items.q: Do I answer every question on Edexcel English Language?
a: Every question in Section A, and only one of the two options in Section B, on both papers. Answering both Section B tasks wastes about forty-five minutes and earns no extra marks.
No. GCSE English Language is untiered on every board, so all students sit the same papers and the full 9 to 1 range is available.

pages.description: Edexcel GCSE English Language Paper 1 explained: the 19th-century fiction extract, the four reading questions with their marks, and the imaginative writing task.
pages.keywords: Edexcel paper 1, fiction and imaginative writing, Edexcel 1EN0/01, Edexcel English Language question 4, Edexcel imaginative writing

hero.text: A 19th-century fiction extract, four reading questions worth 24 marks between them, and one piece of your own writing worth 40. The writing is worth more than all the reading put together.

blocks.title: About the examples on this page
text: Every example and practice task here was written by RCF English. They are **not** Edexcel questions or Edexcel source texts, and no Edexcel mark scheme wording is reproduced. RCF English is not affiliated with, endorsed by or approved by Pearson Edexcel.
Edexcel's own papers and mark schemes are linked on the [papers page](global-english/gcse/edexcel/papers/).

blocks.text: **Paper 1 is called Fiction and Imaginative Writing, paper code 1EN0/01. It lasts 1 hour 45 minutes, carries 64 marks and is worth 40% of the GCSE.** Section A gives you one 19th-century fiction extract of about 650 words and asks four questions worth 24 marks. Section B asks for one piece of imaginative writing worth 40 marks, on a theme linked to the extract.

blocks.heading: The questions
blocks.caption: Marks read from a real Edexcel 1EN0/01 question paper. Section A totals 24 marks.
rows: Identify a phrase from named lines
From named lines, give two things
How the writer uses language and structure to achieve a stated effect
Evaluate how successfully something is achieved in the extract
Imaginative writing - choose one task only

blocks.title: The timings on the paper are Edexcel's; the per-question split is not
text: The paper itself advises about **1 hour on Section A** and about **45 minutes on Section B**. Those are Edexcel's own figures.

Edexcel does not publish a time for each individual question. The minutes in the table above are an RCF recommendation worked out from the marks, and nobody will mark you down for dividing your hour differently.

parts.heading: Question 1 (1 mark) and Question 2 (2 marks)
text: Both are retrieval questions on named lines. Question 1 usually asks for a single phrase; Question 2 asks for two things and may allow your own words or a quotation.
bullets: Answer from the lines named and nowhere else.
For Question 1, quote the phrase exactly. Do not explain it.
For Question 2, give exactly two things, each on its own line.
Three marks in total. Do not spend more than five minutes here.

parts.heading: Question 3: language and structure (6 marks)
text: This is a compact analysis question - six marks, not fifteen - and it names both language *and* structure. An answer that writes only about word choice has left half the question alone.
bullets: Two or three developed points is the right size for 6 marks.
Cover both: at least one point about words or images, and at least one about how the extract is ordered or paced.
Quote briefly and say what the effect is on the reader.
Do not write a fifteen-mark answer here. The time belongs to Question 4.

parts.heading: Question 4: evaluation (15 marks)
text: The question states something the extract attempts - to create strong feelings, to build tension, to make a place seem threatening - and asks you to evaluate how successfully it is achieved. It is the largest reading question on the paper.
Evaluation means judgement. Say how well it works, not only how it is done.
bullets: Open by answering the question: largely successful, partly successful, successful in one way and less so in another.
Three or four developed paragraphs, each with a short quotation and a judgement.
Include one paragraph that qualifies - a place where the effect is weaker, or achieved by a different means than you expected.
Keep referring to the wording of the statement in the question.

parts.heading: Question 5 or 6: imaginative writing (40 marks)
text: Choose **one**. The tasks are linked by a theme to the reading extract, and one of them provides two images to help you generate ideas. Pearson states that you may draw on one image, or neither.

The marks split between communication and organisation on one hand, and vocabulary, sentence structures, spelling and punctuation on the other - the same division you will see described on the [AQA creative writing page](global-english/gcse/aqa/paper-1/creative-writing/), whose method transfers directly.
bullets: Plan for five minutes. Know your last line before you write your first.
The images are a prompt, not a subject to describe item by item.
Four to six paragraphs, with deliberate variation in length.
Leave five minutes to check accuracy. It is a large share of these 40 marks.

blocks.heading: Paper 1 checklist
items: Have I answered Questions 1 and 2 from the named lines only?
Does my Question 3 answer cover **both** language and structure?
Is my Question 3 answer the right size for 6 marks, not 15?
Does my Question 4 answer make a judgement, not just an analysis?
Have I chosen **one** Section B task, not both?
Have I kept 45 minutes for Section B, which is worth more than all of Section A?

items.q: How long is the reading extract on Edexcel Paper 1?
a: Pearson's specification states that the 19th-century fiction extract will be approximately 650 words. There is one extract only, and you meet it for the first time in the examination.

items.q: Do I have to use the images in the writing question?
a: No. Pearson's specification says that one of the writing tasks provides two images to help students generate ideas, and that a student may write a response that draws on just one of the images or on neither. They are a prompt, not a requirement.

items.q: How much should I write for Question 4?
a: Enough for three or four developed paragraphs, which in the 25 minutes or so it deserves is usually about a side. Question 4 is worth 15 of the 24 reading marks on this paper, so it should take well over half your Section A time.

pages.title: Edexcel English Language Paper 2
pages.metaTitle: Edexcel English Language Paper 2: Questions 1-9 Explained | RCF English
pages.description: Edexcel GCSE English Language Paper 2 explained question by question: two non-fiction texts, the 15-mark analysis and evaluation questions, and Question 7a and 7b.
pages.keywords: Edexcel paper 2, non-fiction and transactional writing, Edexcel question 7a 7b, Edexcel 1EN0/02, Edexcel paper 2 marks, Edexcel transactional writing

hero.text: Two hours and five minutes, ninety-six marks, sixty per cent of the qualification. Nine questions, of which you answer eight. This is the paper that decides the grade.

blocks.title: About the examples on this page
text: Every example and practice task here was written by RCF English. They are **not** Edexcel questions or Edexcel source texts, and no Edexcel mark scheme wording is reproduced. RCF English is not affiliated with, endorsed by or approved by Pearson Edexcel.

blocks.text: **Paper 2 is called Non-fiction and Transactional Writing, paper code 1EN0/02. It lasts 2 hours 5 minutes, carries 96 marks and is worth 60% of the GCSE.** Section A gives you two unseen non-fiction extracts - one from the 20th century and one from the 21st, one of them literary non-fiction - and asks seven questions worth 56 marks. Section B asks for one piece of transactional writing worth 40 marks.

blocks.heading: The questions
blocks.caption: Marks read from a real Edexcel 1EN0/02 question paper. Section A totals 56 marks; Section B adds 40.
rows: From named lines, identify two things
From named lines, give two things - own words or quotation
Analyse how the writer uses language and structure to interest and engage the reader
From named lines, identify one thing
From named lines, identify one thing
Evaluate how successfully the writer achieves a stated purpose
What similarities do the two texts share? Use evidence from both
Compare how the writers present ideas and perspectives
Transactional writing - choose one task only

blocks.title: The timings on the paper
text: The paper advises about **1 hour 20 minutes on Section A** and about **45 minutes on Section B**. Those are Edexcel's figures. The per-question minutes in the table are an RCF recommendation derived from the marks.

blocks.heading: The four short questions: six marks in ten minutes
text: Questions 1, 2, 4 and 5 are retrieval, and together they are worth 6 marks. Two are on Text 1 and two on Text 2, and each names the lines you must answer from.
bullets: Answer from the named lines only. Material from elsewhere earns nothing.
Give exactly the number asked for - two things, or one thing.
A short phrase is enough. Full sentences waste time you need for the 15-mark questions.
Questions 4 and 5 are worth one mark each. Do not write a paragraph for one mark.

blocks.heading: Question 3: analyse language and structure (15 marks)
text: On Text 1 only. The question asks how the writer uses language **and** structure to interest and engage the reader. Both words are in the question and both are marked.

parts.heading: A shape that fits 15 marks
numbered: Two paragraphs on language: a short quotation, what the writer is doing, the effect on the reader, then one development.
One paragraph on structure: how the extract opens, where the focus shifts, how it ends.
One further paragraph on either, taken deeper than the others.
Four developed paragraphs is a full answer in about 22 minutes.

parts.heading: What separates the top band
text: Not more quotations. A second reading of a single word - why *that* one rather than the plainer alternative the writer could have used. The [language analysis page](global-english/gcse/aqa/language-analysis/) shows the same quotation answered at three levels.

blocks.heading: Question 6: evaluation (15 marks)
text: On Text 2 only. The question states a purpose the writer attempts - to show the impact of something, to persuade you of something - and asks you to evaluate how successfully it is achieved, supported by detailed reference.
bullets: **Answer the question in your first sentence.** Say how successful, then justify it.
Three or four developed paragraphs, each with a judgement and a short quotation.
Use one paragraph to qualify: something the text does less well, or achieves by an unexpected route.
Analysis without judgement is the commonest way to lose marks here. *The writer uses a metaphor* is analysis; *the metaphor works because it makes an abstract problem physical* is evaluation.

blocks.heading: Question 7: the only question using both texts (20 marks)
text: Question 7 comes in two parts and is worth 20 marks between them. Students routinely treat the two parts as one job. They are not.

parts.heading: 7(a): synthesis, 6 marks
text: This asks what the two texts have in **common**, with evidence from both. It is about content, not method. Do not analyse technique here.
bullets: Three clear similarities is a full answer.
Each one: state the similarity, quote briefly from Text 1, quote briefly from Text 2.
Keep it factual and quick. Six marks in about ten minutes.

parts.heading: 7(b): comparison, 14 marks
text: This asks you to compare how the writers **present** their ideas and perspectives. The paper gives you bullets: the ideas and perspectives, how they are presented, and how they are similar or different.
Now method matters. Both halves - what the writers think and how they show it - are marked.
bullets: Three paragraphs, and **both writers in every paragraph**.
Name the difference in perspective first, then analyse how each writer conveys it.
Use comparative connectives: *where Text 1 asserts, Text 2 concedes*.
End at least one paragraph by weighing the two. The [comparing viewpoints page](global-english/gcse/aqa/comparing-viewpoints/) has a full worked example.

blocks.heading: Section B: transactional writing (40 marks)
text: Choose one of the two tasks. The tasks are linked by a theme to the reading extracts, and Pearson notes that the same form may appear on both tasks with a different focus or audience - so read both before choosing.
Text types include articles, letters, reviews, texts for speeches, and sections for guides, leaflets or booklets.
bullets: Identify the form, the purpose and the audience before you plan anything else.
The form must be visible from the first three lines - a headline, a salutation, an address to an audience.
Plan three arguments and one concession. Five minutes.
Leave five minutes to check accuracy. The [transactional writing method](global-english/gcse/aqa/paper-2/writing/) transfers directly from the AQA page.

blocks.heading: Edexcel Paper 2
do: Check which text each question refers to before answering.
Spend about ten minutes total on Questions 1, 2, 4 and 5.
Give Questions 3 and 6 about twenty minutes each - they are 30 of the 56 reading marks.
Handle both writers in every paragraph of 7(b).
Choose one Section B task and commit to it.
dont: Do not analyse method in 7(a). It asks for similarities of content.
Do not describe technique without judgement in Question 6 - it is an evaluation question.
Do not answer Question 3 on Text 2, or Question 6 on Text 1.
Do not write both Section B tasks.
Do not run Section A over time. Section B is 40 marks and it comes last.

items.q: What is the difference between Question 7a and 7b on Edexcel Paper 2?
a: Question 7(a) is worth 6 marks and asks what similarities the two texts share, using evidence from both. It is about content. Question 7(b) is worth 14 marks and asks you to compare how the writers present ideas and perspectives, so it needs analysis of method as well as content. Answering 7(b) as a second synthesis caps the mark.

items.q: How many marks is Edexcel English Language Paper 2?
a: 96 marks in total: 56 for Section A reading and 40 for Section B writing. The paper is worth 60% of the GCSE, and it lasts 2 hours 5 minutes.

items.q: How long are the two texts on Edexcel Paper 2?
a: Pearson's specification states that the word count across the two extracts will be approximately 1,000 words, and that the minimum length of an extract will be 300 words. One text is from the 20th century and one from the 21st, and one of the two is literary non-fiction.

items.q: Which questions on Edexcel Paper 2 are worth the most?
a: Question 3 and Question 6 are worth 15 marks each, and Question 7 is worth 20 marks across its two parts. Those three questions carry 50 of the 56 reading marks. The four short retrieval questions carry 6 marks between them.
